stories.title: Showcase: EO for Ecosystems and Biodiversity
stories.description: Mapping, monitoring and valuing nature with EO

content.title: Introduction
content.description:
Earth Observation (EO) gathers information about the planet’s land and oceans, mostly from satellites, with field data used to validate it.

ESA missions and the EU’s [Copernicus](https://www.copernicus.eu)  programme provide free, regular acquired images of the whole planet in optical, thermal and radar wavelengths. Combined with field data and models, this makes it possible to map land cover, habitats and track indicators of their condition and see how they change, consistently, across countries and over days to decades.

For biodiversity, EO does not count species directly. It helps map the habitats that species depend on, some of the pressures acting on them, and the changes related to protection or restoration. Combined with field data, EO-based products give site managers, statisticians and policy makers a shared, repeatable evidence base.

This story walks through eleven examples, from global maps down to single protected sites.

content.title: Mapping land cover: the first step
content.description:
Knowing what covers the land, whether forest, grassland, wetland or cropland, is the first step towards mapping ecosystems and the habitats that species depend on. 

ESA's [WorldCover](https://esa-worldcover.org) map, built from Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 optical data, sorts the world's land into 11 cover classes at 10 m spatial resolution, including tree cover, grassland, wetlands, mangroves and built-up areas. 

The great forest belts of the Amazon, Congo and boreal north stand out in green, next to the cropland regions of North America, Europe and South Asia. 

In Europe, the [Copernicus Land Monitoring Service](https://land.copernicus.eu) produces similar Sentinel-based maps at 10 m, such as the [CLC+ Backbone](https://land.copernicus.eu/api/en/products/clc-backbone/clc-backbone-2021) for 2021, tailored to the continent's requirements. 

Combined with climate, terrain and field data, land cover is used to map ecosystem types, as the next step shows.

content.title: From land cover to ecosystem accounts
content.description:
In Europe, satellite-based maps combined with other data support the ecosystem statistics that countries are starting to report.

The ESA-funded [PEOPLE-EA](https://eo4society.esa.int/projects/people-ea/) project combined EO, including Copernicus land cover, with other spatial data to map ecosystem types across Greece, following the European EUNIS habitat classification. The map separates forests, heathland and scrub, grasslands, wetlands, coastal habitats and built-up areas such as Athens.

The same map can be summarised for any administrative region. Click through the NUTS 2 and NUTS 3 levels to see how regions change in their forest, heathland and scrub and man-made vegetated habitats cover. 

Such figures follow the UN [SEEA Ecosystem Accounting](https://seea.un.org/ecosystem-accounting) standard, which EU Member States will report under the 2024 update of EU rules on environmental accounts.

content.title: Taking the pulse of vegetation
content.description:
From the sunlight that plants reflect, satellites are able to estimate the greenness and density of vegetation, every few days, where clouds allow.

The [Copernicus Land Monitoring Service](https://land.copernicus.eu) provides several such indicators from Sentinel-2. NDVI compares red and near-infrared reflectance and is a widely used proxy for vegetation greenness and vigour. The Leaf Area Index (LAI) estimates leaf area per unit of ground, and FAPAR shows the share of sunlight that plants absorb for photosynthesis.

Tracked over seasons and years, these indicators can signal drought stress, recovery after fires or storms, and long-term changes in vegetation condition, one part of overall ecosystem condition.

content.title: Peatlands: hidden carbon and biodiversity stores
content.description:
Peatlands cover a small share of the world's land but store a disproportionately large share of its soil carbon, and they provide a home for specialised plants and animals.

The [Global Peatlands Initiative](https://www.unep.org/topics/peatlands/peatland-mapping) compiles national and global datasets, including those from satellites, to show where peatlands are present, from the boreal north to the tropics. In the United Kingdom they include the upland blanket bogs of various sites.

At Moor House National Nature Reserve in the North Pennines, the ESA-funded [WorldPeatland](https://eo4society.esa.int/projects/worldpeatland/) project estimated peatland water level trends for 2017–2024 from satellite data. Falling levels can indicate drying and a risk of carbon loss. The project also developed a satellite-based peat health index, validated with field data, to help site managers target and check restoration such as blocking drainage ditches. See the SEF use case [Restoring and Conserving Peatlands](https://sef.apex.esa.int/en/use-cases/Restoring-and-Conserving-Peatlands).

content.title: Soil carbon in protected sites
content.description:
Soils are one of the largest carbon stores on land, and their health underpins plant and animal life above ground.

The ESA-funded [WorldSoils](https://eo4society.esa.int/projects/worldsoils/) project estimated organic carbon in the top 20 cm of soil across Europe at 100 m resolution (2020–2022), by combining satellite data with soil samples and models.

In the explorer, statistics can be extracted for Natura 2000 sites. In Ķemeri National Park in Latvia, home to the Great Ķemeri Bog, the chart shows how much of the site falls into each soil carbon range. A WorldCover breakdown of the same site shows 72% tree cover and 15% herbaceous wetland, linking habitat type to likely carbon storage.

content.title: Weighing the forests from space
content.description:
Radar satellites see through clouds and, depending on their wavelength, partly into forest canopies. With models and field plots, their signal is used to estimate how much wood forests hold.

This above-ground biomass map from the ESA-funded [Forest Carbon Monitoring](https://eo4society.esa.int/projects/forest-carbon-monitoring) project combines Sentinel-1 and ALOS-2 radar data at 20 m. Biomass is a proxy for carbon stocks and for forest structure, which shapes habitat quality for many species.

content.title: Forest biomass by country and region
content.description:
The above-ground biomass map can be summarised for countries and regions, and is shown here for Romania. Click on the country to see more detailed statistics.

Romania's Carpathians show some of the highest biomass values in Europe. ESA's [Biomass](https://www.esa.int/Applications/Observing_the_Earth/FutureEO/Biomass/ESA_s_Biomass_goes_live_with_data_now_open_to_all) mission, launched in 2025, is the first satellite to carry a P-band radar, which can penetrate dense forest canopies to give better estimates of biomass.

content.title: Seeing change over time
content.description:
Because satellites revisit the same place again and again, they can show how land cover and habitats change over days, weeks, years and decades.

Doñana in southern Spain is one of Europe's most important wetlands and a Natura 2000 site under pressure from water use, agriculture and wildfire. The [CLMS Natura 2000](https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/n2k/n2k-2018) product maps 55 land cover and land use classes for 2006, 2012 and 2018 in 4,790 grassland-rich Natura 2000 sites, interpreted from very high spatial resolution satellite imagery.

Comparing 2012 and 2018 shows coastal pine forest turning into “damaged forest” in the north-west of the site. This matches the Las Peñuelas wildfire of June 2017, which burned about 8,500 ha between Mazagón and the Asperillo dune. For longer trends, ESA's [Climate Change Initiative land cover](https://climate.esa.int/en/projects/land-cover/) series of products goes back to 1992, and Sentinel-2 images show the area as the eye would see it.

content.title: Reading the ocean's living conditions
content.description:
Healthy marine life depends on stable temperature, salinity and food supply regimes.

The [Copernicus Marine Service](https://marine.copernicus.eu) combines satellite and in-situ observations with ocean models to produce daily global maps. Satellites observe properties of the ocean surface, such as temperature, ocean colour and, more coarsely, salinity; with the conditions at depth coming from the models.

Chlorophyll-a maps, derived from ocean colour, indicate where phytoplankton, the base of the marine food web, is abundant, for example in the upwelling zones off West Africa and South America. Together with temperature, salinity and modelled zooplankton, such indicators describe the context for marine biodiversity and can support the planning of marine protected areas and fisheries.

content.title: Oosterschelde (The Netherlands): a coastal Natura 2000 site
content.description:
At the scale of a single site, EO can describe both the pressures on a coastal ecosystem and its physical condition.

The Oosterschelde estuary in the Netherlands is a Natura 2000 site whose tidal flats feed large numbers of wading birds. The ESA-funded [PEOPLE-EA](https://eo4society.esa.int/projects/people-ea/) project mapped the share of artificial, sealed surfaces along its beaches, dunes and wetlands, a pressure indicator used in coastal condition accounts.

content.title: Tracking the tidal flats
content.description:
The intertidal flats are only exposed, and visible from space, at low tide.

The ESA-funded [EO4Ports](https://eo4ports.earsc.org/) project mapped the low water line from Landsat and Sentinel-2 images combined with tidal models, separating water, wet sand and land. The normalised difference water index (NDWI) built only from low-tide images, available for 2021 and 2025, and a tide line series for 2022–2025 help delineate the extent of the intertidal flats over time. Following the changes in their extent helps managers spot loss or erosion of habitats that birds and shellfish depend on.

content.title: Supporting policy: Land Degradation Neutrality
content.description:
EO helps countries report on global commitments, such as the UN Sustainable Development Goal of a land degradation-neutral world (SDG 15.3).

Progress is measured with [three sub-indicators](https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/library/1768_UNCCD_GPG_SDG-Indicator-15.3.1_version2_2021.pdf): trends in land cover, land productivity and carbon stocks. The ESA-funded [SEN4LDN](https://sdg.esa.int/sen4ldn) project derived these mainly from Sentinel-2 data at 10 m spatial resolution, with biomass change as a proxy for carbon stocks. This is far more detailed than the existing global default datasets.

Around Serra da Estrela, a protected mountain area in Portugal dominated by grassland (59%) and tree cover (36%), the map separates areas that recovered between 2018 and 2023 from those that degraded, including wildfire scars. National authorities can use such maps to report to the UN Convention to Combat Desertification and to target restoration.

content.title: Biodiversity in the national economy
content.description:
EO-based land-use maps, combined with biodiversity models, can help to bring nature into economic decision making.

The [LEON](https://www.leon-naturefinance.org/) project, led by the University of Oxford and Assimila, mapped the [Biodiversity Intactness Index](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/our-science/services/data/biodiversity-intactness-index.html) for Denmark every year from 2017 to 2022. Annual maps estimating how much terrestrial biodiversity remains relative to minimally used primary vegetation in Denmark. The index combines relative abundance with similarity in species composition. Values close to 1 indicate greater intactness.

It supports biodiversity monitoring, planning and natural capital accounting.

content.title: Find out more
content.description:
This showcase gave an overview of how EO supports work on ecosystems and biodiversity, from global maps to single protected sites.

Many more datasets and tools are available from ESA-funded projects, the Copernicus services and commercial providers. Please contact the [Stakeholder Engagement Facility](https://sef.apex.esa.int/) team to discuss your needs.

content.title: Introduction
content.description:
Doñana, at the mouth of the Guadalquivir river in south-western Spain, is one of Europe's most important wetlands. Its marshes, lagoons, dunes and pine forests are protected as a national park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site (since 1994) and a Natura 2000 site, and it has long been a wintering ground for hundreds of thousands of waterbirds.

Doñana is under strong pressure. Less water reaches its marshes and lagoons because of a changing climate and groundwater extraction, much of it for intensive irrigation around the park. In 2024, the number of wintering waterbirds fell to about 123,000, the lowest in 25 years ([IUCN World Heritage Outlook](https://worldheritageoutlook.iucn.org/node/1048)).

This true colour image from Copernicus Sentinel-2 shows the Guadalquivir estuary and the Doñana area as the eye would see it, surrounded by farmland and towns.

A [University of Seville study](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-7086/5/4/75) from December 2025 based on satellite imagery found that Doñana lost about 15% of its average wet area, water volume and water depth between 2005 and 2024. If current trends continue, the authors project that the marshland could disappear within about 60 years.

content.title: Land cover across Europe at 10 m spatial resolution
content.description:
The [Copernicus Land Monitoring Service](https://land.copernicus.eu) maps land cover across Europe at 10 m spatial resolution from Sentinel data. Its [CLC+ Backbone](https://land.copernicus.eu/api/en/products/clc-backbone/clc-backbone-2021) for 2021 sorts every pixel into 11 basic classes.

Around Doñana, it separates water and wetlands, herbaceous vegetation, pine forests (needle-leaved trees), shrubland and the sealed surfaces of towns. Because the same method is used everywhere, the area can be compared consistently with any other part of Europe.

content.title: A closer look at the Natura 2000 site
content.description:
For selected Natura 2000 sites, Copernicus provides a much more detailed [land cover and land use product](https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/n2k/n2k-2018) with 55 classes. It is produced by visual interpretation of very high resolution satellite imagery, with a minimum mapping unit of 0.5 ha, for 2006, 2012 and 2018.

In Doñana, it distinguishes the inland marshes, beaches and dunes, natural pine forests, plantations and agricultural land, which helps site managers follow how each habitat develops.

content.title: Seeing change over time
content.description:
Because the product is available for several years, changes can be compared directly. The swipe tool shows 2006 on one side and 2018 on the other.

Along the coast north-west of the park, between Mazagón and the Asperillo dune, the Las Peñuelas wildfire of June 2017 burned about 8,500 ha ([eldiario.es](https://www.eldiario.es/andalucia/huelva/incendio-calcino-donana-8-000-hectareas-choca-muro-judicial-avances-nueve-anos_1_13321192.html)). The 2018 map shows parts of the coastal pine forest there as "damaged forest".

content.title: Carbon in the soil
content.description:
Soils store large amounts of carbon, and their organic matter supports the plants and animals above ground. The ESA-funded [WorldSoils](https://eo4society.esa.int/projects/worldsoils/) project estimated organic carbon in the top 20 cm of soil across Europe at 100 m resolution (2020–2022) by combining satellite data with soil samples and models.

Around Doñana, the mostly sandy and agricultural soils show low topsoil organic carbon. Some areas, including parts of the marshes and pine forests, have no estimate in this product.

content.title: Soil carbon statistics for the Natura 2000 site
content.description:
Statistics can be extracted for any Natura 2000 site in the explorer. For the Doñana site, the chart shows how much of the mapped area falls into each soil carbon range: most of it lies in the lower ranges, with a smaller share of higher values.

Combined with land cover and habitat maps, such figures help site managers see where carbon-rich soils and habitats coincide, and where protection or restoration could matter most.

Normalised Difference Water Index.   The satellite images captured at low tide (bottom 30% of the springs tidal range) are used to compute a composite NDWI (Normalized Difference Water Index) image. The 70th percentile is taken when calculating the composite to give more weight to dry pixels.

This layer shows a time series of the Low Tide line from 2022 to 2025.  The contour was derived from all the low-tide cloud-free Landsat and Sentinel-2 images available.

For each section of contour, the data available in the layer comprises:
* *id*: unique identifier of the line
* *date*: date of the low tide event
* *springs_tide_range*: the mean springs tidal range at this location according to the FES2022 tidal model
* *obs_tide_level*: observed tide level across the satellite images used (average)
* *images_in_composite*: number of satellite images used to create the composite for this line
